title: DICTO Solids: Exact Geometry
description: Exact geometry of the named polyhedra found or named by DICTO (artist, Osaka) in his published papers and the Kaleidohedra findings archive: 41 solids, among them the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron, the DICTO Truncated-Icosahedral Hecatodihedron, the DICTO OG family of #39, the DBT and OTT, the DICTO Jewel, the DICTO OCD Stella, DICTO's skewed parallelohedra, the six DICTONIC SOLIDS of #48 and #51 (Icosaxes, Unborn Axes, Lotus Jewel Axes, Dodecaxes, Samson and Delilah) and, new in version 3, twelve solids of #55, #56, #57 and #59: Goliath and David, Sonsam and Lahdeli, Ian Dury and Blockhead, Chucky, Fang and the Triskelion Tetrahedron, and Keyaxes, the Icosaxes Hexa and the Lotus Hexa. Every coordinate is exact, in ℚ, ℚ(√5), ℚ(∛2) (Samson and Delilah) or ℚ(t) (Sonsam and Lahdeli, t the root of an irreducible cubic), and also given to 15 decimals; each solid comes with its faces (consistently wound), f-vector, exact volume, squared edge lengths, symmetry group and the values stated in its paper, as JSON and OFF, plus a copy scaled to volume 1. Also included: 6 packings that fill space (the three lattice packings of DICTO's skewed solids and the three DICTONIC BONDS: golden, keyed and Delian) and 4 published packings that do not fill space, each with exact lattice vectors and exact placements of its pieces; and an inventory (index.csv) of all 135 rows of shapes DICTO has named, with finding number, paper, status (new, rediscovered or known), prior art and a universal number: established catalogue numbers (Johnson, uniform, Wenninger, Hart, Mosseri–Sadoc) where they exist, and DICTO's own permanent catalogue numbers D1–D83 for his new shapes, in order of first publication. A standalone checker (check.py, Python 3 + sympy) re-proves every stated value from the data files alone: 998 checks, all passing, including closed outward-wound surfaces, exact planarity, convexity where stated, symmetry, the non-convex keyed solids as their convex hulls minus or plus 8 Tricaps, the non-convex solids of #59 as exact unions of placed dataset solids with Tricap dents and keys, the cubic field of Sonsam and Lahdeli (irreducible, one root in its interval, every sign decided exactly), and exact separating planes showing that the pieces of each packing do not overlap. Shapes and names by DICTO; data built and checked with Claude (Anthropic). More at dictospheres.com .

title: DICTO: Collected Geometric Works
description: DICTO is a geometric sculptor in Osaka. The work grows out of building with recycled PET bottles and from three open apps on one shared geometry: Kaleidohedra, Rhombiverse and Polyhedraverse. This record gathers all of DICTO's published geometry in one place. It opens with a short essay, Quanta of Space , which reads the works as a study of the pieces from which space is built, from the atoms of the ancients (Democritus, Plato's Timaeus ) to the quanta of modern physics (loop quantum gravity), and as a bridge between periodic and aperiodic order. The papers follow in four chapters: Atoms (new solids), Bonds (how pieces fill space), Shells (layers round a core) and Cycles (rules that turn one shell into the next). Each paper has its own DICTO DOI, which always opens its newest version; the numbers (#1, #2 …) are the paper numbers on dictospheres.com; DICTO's findings are numbered separately, F1, F2 …. title: The Icosaxes Hexa: Bloom, Bud and Seed
description: In short. The DICTO Hexa (#18) is eight DICTO Jewels that pass into each other until they close into one block. DICTO asked for the same move with icosahedral symmetry. Twenty Icosaxes, DICTO's golden truncated octahedra (#48), placed on the corners of a dodecahedron and slid towards the centre first touch as the Icosaxes Bloom, with twelve windows (at distance φ²√3/2); at exactly 1/φ of that distance the windows close into the Icosaxes Bud, sealed round a hollow; at exactly one third the hollow fills: the Icosaxes Seed, one solid (with Lotus Jewel Axes: at 1/φ³). Proved exactly. In the lattice, eight Icosaxes round an Unborn Axes make one solid (the same as nine Icosaxes passing through each other, along the whole golden bond from Kelvin onwards), and these blocks form a Kagome network in which every Icosaxes is shared by exactly two blocks; keyed with Tricaps, its piece has volume exactly φ². The idea is DICTO's; the names are DICTO's working names. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic); a first draft by a local open model (gpt-oss-120b), checked line by line. title: DICTO Janus c/h Pyrochlore
description: In short. The pyrochlore network, small tetrahedra touching only at their corners, hides inside every diamond-like crystal: the middles of the bonds round each atom make one tetrahedron. Diamond-like crystals stack their layers in many orders, so the pyrochlore network can too. Sharing out all of space round it by one weight, as in #57 (The Rule of Halves), we prove the same rule: in every close-packed stacking and for every weight from −11/36 to 1/4, every piece is borrowed from the pure cubic or the pure hexagonal stacking — balls by their own layer, diamond atoms by their nearest layer, the two empty holes of each gap as two halves by the layers on their sides. Exact weight walks for the cubic and hexagonal stackings (the cubic one passes through the tetrahedral–truncated tetrahedral honeycomb). Proof with #57's exact engine: locality over sixteen windows and every stretch of the walk (384 of 384), with an independent exact check at twelve weights (768 of 768). The idea is DICTO's. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic); a first draft by a local open model (gpt-oss-120b), checked line by line. Sources checked are listed in the paper. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com .

title: From the Octet to Every Stacking: the Web of Bonds
description: In short. Pile up oranges and there are small gaps between them, of two shapes, arranged according to how the layers are stacked. Over ten papers (#40–#57) DICTO and collaborators asked how the space is shared out into solid pieces, and which pieces touch which. This series paper tells that story, from DICTO's PET-bottle-cap DICTOspheres and the Polyhedraverse app, through the Golden Split, the Delian Bond, the web of bonds and the named pairs David and Goliath and Sonsam and Lahdeli, to the rule of halves: however layers of equal balls are stacked, the space between and around them is shared out into pieces of only finitely many kinds, each borrowed, whole or in half, from the cubic and the hexagonal stackings. Each part ends with the exact statement proved in the paper it retells; no new results are claimed. The ideas and names are DICTO's. Telling and checking with Claude (Anthropic); a first draft and a referee reading by a local open model (gpt-oss-120b), checked line by line against the papers. Photographs of DICTO's sculptures: DICTO. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com . View in the app: https://kaleidohedra.dictospheres.com/?open=stackings:4H

title: The Rule of Halves: the Holes of Every Close-Packed Stacking
description: In short. Stack layers of balls and the gaps between them are small octahedra and tetrahedra. Stack them in the cubic way (ABCABC…) or the hexagonal way (ABAB…) and these gaps are arranged differently; crystals also use countless mixed stackings, such as ABAC or ABCACB. In papers #51, #53 and #56 we slid one number, a weight, between the two kinds of gap and followed how space is shared out among them: the web of bonds. Here we follow it on every stacking at once, and find a simple rule. A tetrahedral gap always takes the piece it would have in the pure stacking of the layer it sits closest to. An octahedral gap sits half-way between two layers, and its piece is two halves: the top half is the top half of the cubic or the hexagonal piece, as the layer above decides, and the bottom half likewise from the layer below. So every stacking, of any length or pattern, is built from the two pure ones, and the kinds of piece are finite: we list them all, with exact volumes. Where a cubic layer meets a hexagonal one, octahedral pieces appear that are half cubic and half hexagonal, which DICTO calls the Janus c/h pieces ; two of them he named Chucky and Fang ; and its volume is exactly the mean of its two parents'. The proof is exact, with one bound done by hand. The rule was not found in the sources checked; its classical counterpart for the balls themselves, that each ball's surroundings are set by its own layer, is the reason the h/c notation of crystallography exists. The ideas are DICTO's: following the web of bonds onto the other close-packed stackings (25 October 2026), and the names Chucky, Fang and Triskelion Tetrahedron, and the set name Janus c/h pieces. Computation, exact proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic); a first draft by a local open model (gpt-oss-120b) was used for the order of sections only. Exact studies, checks, scripts and the appendix data attached (commit b24fd15d). Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com . title: Sonsam and Lahdeli: the Delian Bond on the Twinned Octet, with Ian Dury, Blockhead and Keyed Switch Points
description: In short. This paper is about webs of bonds: when pieces fill space, each shared face is a bond, and the bonds together make a network that rewires as the pieces change (#52, #53). Here we follow that network on a second stacking, and show that keys change the pieces but never the network. Stack layers of balls in the cubic way (ABCABC…) and the gaps between them are octahedra and tetrahedra: the octet. Stack them in the hexagonal way (ABAB…), each layer a mirror image of its neighbours across it, and the gaps are the same octahedra and tetrahedra, joined across the mirror planes: the twinned octet. Paper #53 slid one number, a weight, between the two kinds of gap and recorded every way space splits on the way. On the cubic octet, at one exact weight, λ = 3/8 − ∛4/4 (the cube root of 2, squared: the number of the Delian problem, doubling the cube), the two pieces have equal volume: DICTO's Samson and Delilah. We follow the same walk on the twinned octet. It has its own equal-volume point, at the single root of an irreducible cubic; there the two pieces are new solids, which DICTO named Sonsam (19 corners, one face a nine-sided polygon lying on the mirror plane) and Lahdeli (12 corners), the syllables swapped as the stacking is mirrored. Further on, the twinned walk makes a stop the cubic walk does not have: Ian Dury (16 corners) with the classical 60° rhombohedron; and where the cubic walk ends in cubes the twinned one ends in Blockheads (10 corners), the twin of the cube. Every volume is exact: √2/6, 13√2/54, √2/54, √2/4. Moving a cap from one piece into its neighbour keeps the tiling and its web of bonds; done with the new pairs this gives DICTO's keyed forms Sonsam-K and Lahdeli-K, and Ian Dury-K with Rhombo-K, a six-pointed star. Finally we read DICTO's Sunstar lattice (#42) in the same light: it is rock salt's switch point (#53) keyed with Euclid's roofs. The two new walks' pieces and the keyed forms were not found in the sources checked. The ideas are DICTO's: that further bonds may be "hiding in plain sight" in the census networks; other rhythms of volume (doubling, tripling); a different but cohesive bond network beside the golden and Delian ones; keyed versions of the new pairs; and the names Sonsam, Lahdeli, Ian Dury, Blockhead and the -K forms (25 October 2026). Computation, exact proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). Exact studies and checks attached (commit ca73df8). Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com .

title: One Turn Is a Gnomon: the Golden Cycle Step by Step, and the Polar of the Keyed Pair
description: In short. Take a square of 3 × 3 dots and add an L-shaped strip of 3 + 4 dots along two sides: you get the next square, 4 × 4. The strip is a gnomon: in the classical definition (Euclid, and Heron in general), the piece which, added to a figure, makes a whole of the same shape as the figure, only larger. The gnomon method as reported for Júlia Pimentel works with exactly this strip, n + (n + 1). DICTO's idea was to carry that structure into three dimensions: walk through his golden cycle of twelve nested solids, from an icosahedron out to the next icosahedron φ³ times larger, and check at every step what it adds and whether the new whole has the shape of something before it. We built every step exactly. The answer is clean. The whole turn is a classical gnomon: the next icosahedron has the same shape as the first. No single step and no shorter run of steps is: no station has the shape of any other station, except the two icosahedra. So it is the last step, from M to the next icosahedron, that closes the gnomon. Step by step, the cycle adds spikes, pyramids, Shields and other pieces that never repeat their shapes. By volume, four steps still add a clean golden amount. DICTO's second idea concerned his keyed pair of space-filling pieces, the Lotus Jewel Axes (eight dents) and the Dodecaxes (eight keys). A dented or keyed solid has no ordinary polar, so DICTO's method is to fill the dents in (or take the keys off), take the polar of the smooth solid, and keep what was removed as the remainder. The smooth solids are the golden pair of paper #48; their polars are cubes with a low pyramid on every face, of heights 1/φ and 1/φ², which add up to exactly 1, the height that makes Kepler's rhombic dodecahedron; and the remainder is the same eight Tricaps for both pieces. Both parts read a solid by the piece that lies between it and its neighbour. Theorem A (the classical gnomon of the golden cycle). In the cycle I ⊂ Cleo star ⊂ D′ ⊂ ID ⊂ OG ⊂ rTI ⊂ TI ⊂ H ⊂ jtI ⊂ RT ⊂ M ⊂ I·φ³ the only two similar stations are I and I·φ³ (ratio φ³). Hence one whole turn, I·φ³ minus I, is a classical gnomon of I; no single step and no shorter run of steps is a classical gnomon; and, within the turn from I, the last step, M → I·φ³, is the only step whose new whole is similar to an earlier station. Table 4 lists what each step adds. Corollary (volumes). Every station is an exact multiple a + b√5 of I; Cleo star = 2·I, RT = 81·I/φ², M = φ⁸·I, I·φ³ = φ·M; exactly four steps (1, 6, 7, 11) add a rational multiple of φ k ·I. Theorem B (the keyed pair, hull and remainder). The Lotus Jewel Axes and the Dodecaxes are the Icosaxes and the Unborn Axes minus and plus the same eight Tricaps, each of volume 1/(12φ²). The polar of the Icosaxes is a cube with six face pyramids of height 1/φ (in half cube edges), that of the Unborn Axes one with height 1/φ²; along the whole factor-x family of the two heights are x/(1 + x) and 1/(1 + x), so they always add up to 1, the rhombic dodecahedron's height. A polar of the Lotus Jewel Axes taken face by face about one centre would put spikes over the eight dents. All results are exact (119 checks, none failed). The ideas are DICTO's: carrying the "add the next strip" structure of the gnomon method as reported for Júlia Pimentel, n² + n + (n + 1) = (n + 1)², into his three-dimensional golden cycle, and judging each step by the shape it adds as well as by its volume; the names Julias and Pimentels are DICTO's; the hull-and-remainder polar of the keyed pair, "fill them in, maybe invert, then work out the remainder" (DICTO, 24 October 2026); and, from his earlier papers, the twelve-station golden cycle, the Cleo star, the DICTONIC SOLIDS and their names. title: David and Goliath: Jessen's Icosahedron and the Tetrahedron in the A15 Weight Walk
description: In short. Paper #53 slid one number, a weight, between the two kinds of points of ten crystal arrangements and recorded, exactly, every tiling of space that appears on the way. In the A15 alloy structure (the arrangement of Cr 3 Si, and of the Weaire–Phelan foam) one stop stood out: at weight difference 3/4 the space-filling pieces are a 20-faced icosahedron around every Si point and a small tetrahedron around every Cr point. DICTO named the pair Goliath and David. Here we prove the stop exactly and identify Goliath: its corners are exactly those of Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron, so Goliath is that famous non-convex solid's convex hull. Goliath has the same shape as the classical Z12 icosahedron of A15 (Frank and Kasper), and the whole tiling is the classical picture of A15 as icosahedra and tetrahedral holes, moved by half a body diagonal; that picture is known. What we did not find in the sources searched is that the weight walk lands exactly on it, at 3/4, and the plain statement that the A15 icosahedron is Jessen's convex hull. We then place David and Goliath among the known pairs that the same walks produce: the octet, octahedra with cuboctahedra, the Weaire–Phelan cells, rock salt's equilateral chamfered cubes with cubes, and zinc blende's capped octahedra with regular tetrahedra. The ideas are DICTO's: the names David and Goliath (25 October 2026), and DICTO's idea of pursuing the icosahedral pairing found in the census of paper #53, together with the framing that a new pairing shows something new while known pairs support the theorem further; computation, exact proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). title: The Web of Bonds: How the DICTONIC Bonds Hand Over
description: In short. DICTO's two loops of space-filling pairs, the golden loop of paper #48 and the Delian loop of paper #51, each slide one pair of solids through a whole family of shapes. Draw one line, a bond, between every two pieces that share a face, and the lines make a web. We show that each loop is really one fixed crowd of points of two kinds, the piece centres, and that the only thing that moves is one number, a weight given to one kind against the other. Every piece is the region nearer (in this weighted sense) to its own point than to any other. Then the web is exactly the web of the classical weighted Delaunay construction. As the weight slides, the bond between unlike pieces never breaks. The two like bonds hand over: in the golden loop gradually, both alive all the way and equal at Kelvin's cell; in the Delian loop all at once, at the octet, where every rhombus of a hidden rhombic dodecahedron trades its long diagonal for its short one. Read physically, the weight is a ball radius squared: the golden loop is the caesium chloride structure, the Delian loop the fluorite structure, and the range where the balls can touch is bounded exactly by Pauling's classical radius-ratio limits (the same contact condition as Pauling's). Main theorem. For every x in [0, ∞] the golden network is the power diagram of the body-centred cubic sites with weight difference (φ²/4)(x − 1)/(x + 1); for every t in [0, 1] the Delian network is the power diagram of the fluorite sites with weight difference (3/8)(2t − 1). The web is the 1-skeleton of the dual regular subdivision, with exact bond areas. At the ends, at Kelvin's cell and at the octet these are classical Voronoi or Delaunay tessellations; the theorem gives the whole family between them. In the golden loop all three bond types live on the whole open loop, with constant face lattice; the two like bonds have area ratio x² and are equal only at x = 1. In the Delian loop the unlike bond lives exactly on (0, 1), oct–oct exactly on [0, 1/3), tet–tet exactly on (1/3, 1]; t = 1/3, the octet, is the only parameter at which both pieces exist and only one bond type is present. Theorem 2 (the balls): the weight is a squared radius; with unlike neighbours touching, ρ = (x + 2)/(2x + 1) and ρ = t/(1 − t), and the touching windows end exactly at Pauling's limits √3 − 1 and √(3/2) − 1 (Pauling's own contact condition, rederived). All geometric results are exact (371 + 61 checks, none failed; the 24 physical checks of the scale-anomaly study are estimates). The ideas are DICTO's: the DICTONIC SOLIDS and the DICTONIC BONDS and their names, and the web of bonds, a network of bonds that "should create a web of lattices that change with the rhythm of the loop" (DICTO, 25 October 2026); computation, exact proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). title: One Move Each: Classical Cut-and-Glue Space-Fillers Built Exactly
description: In short. Books describe several classical solids that fill space by how to make them from other solids: shave a belt off one, stick two pyramids onto another, glue a few slanted bricks together. Kaleidohedra makes the same solids in one go, by tilting and stretching a lattice of points, and so gives every corner and every volume exactly. The moves themselves are Fedorov's (1885); what this paper adds is the exact data, the settings and the proofs. Main theorem. Five space-fillers that the literature gives by cutting, gluing, zone removal or a drawing are each obtained exactly by one setting of Kaleidohedra's three moves: a shear of the lattice, the equal-edged cell (Cell = 1) and a stretch along a free direction. With edge 1: the regular-hexagon elongated dodecahedron, volume 4√2, symmetry D2h; the Bain rhombic dodecahedron, 2√2, D4h; the classical elongated dodecahedron, 8/3 + 16√3/9, D4h; the Bilinski dodecahedron, (4/5)√(5 + 2√5), D2h; and the 60° rhombohedron, 1/√2, D3d. Each tiles space by translation and is congruent, corner by corner, to its classical construction. Theorem 2: every rhombic-dodecahedron-type cell has exactly three free directions. The Bilinski dodecahedron is glued exactly from two acute and two obtuse golden rhombohedra, and DICTO's skewed rhombic dodecahedron (F1) is a linear image of it. The idea, that Kaleidohedra's lattice moves rebuild exactly the space-fillers the literature gives by cutting and gluing, is DICTO's, as are his skewed rhombic dodecahedron (F1) and his route to the regular-hexagon elongated dodecahedron (F5); computation, proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). More at dictospheres.com .

title: The Delian Bond: Samson, Delilah and the Octet Between Kepler's Rhombic Dodecahedron and the Cube
description: In short. Regular tetrahedra and octahedra fill space together: the octet. Join each tetrahedron's centre to each octahedron's centre through the face they share, cut every such double cone by one flat plane parallel to that face, and give each side to its own centre. Slide the cut, and every position still fills space with two convex solids, from Kepler's rhombic dodecahedra through the octet to cubes. At one position the two solids have exactly the same volume: the tetrahedron's piece has doubled and the octahedron's halved, the doubling of the ancient Delian problem in both directions at once. DICTO named this pair Samson and Delilah. Main theorem. For every cut position t from 0 to 1 the two pieces are convex and fill space face to face: for t ≤ 1/3 a regular tetrahedron of edge 3t and a rhombic dodecahedron with its eight three-fold corners cut, for t ≥ 1/3 a regular octahedron of edge 3(1 − t)/2 and a cube with four alternate corners cut, with exact volumes. Theorem 2: at t = (2√6 − 3)/15 and t = 5/3 − (2/3)√2 every edge is equal; at t = 1 − ∛6/3 the two kinds each fill half of space. Theorem 3 (the Delian bond): at t = 1 − (2/3)·2 −1/3 , and only there, the two pieces have equal volume: Samson, the cut cube, twice the octet's tetrahedron, and Delilah, a regular octahedron, half the octet's octahedron. Exact in ℚ(√6), ℚ(√2), ℚ(∛2) and ℚ(∛6). With paper #48 this gives DICTO's six DICTONIC SOLIDS in three DICTONIC BONDS (golden, keyed, Delian). Not all six are new as shapes; what is new is each bond. A remark shows that the same weighted cut for the cube meets only known solids (truncated cubic, rectified cubic and Kelvin's honeycombs), so the count stays at three bonds; another remark gives the polar pair of #48. The family through the octet, its equal-edged and half-and-half members and the Delian bond were not found in the sources checked. The ideas, and the names Samson, Delilah, DICTONIC SOLIDS and DICTONIC BONDS, are DICTO's; computation, exact proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). More at dictospheres.com . title: The Golden Split: Icosahedra, Unborns and AXE Become Two Convex Space-Fillers
description: In short. Icosahedra cannot fill space on their own. Set them in a cubic grid, edge to edge, and two kinds of gap are left: a squeezed icosahedron (the Unborn) in the middle of each cube, and thin tetrahedra (the AXE) between them. Cut each AXE into four pyramids from the point 1/φ of the way along its axis and give each pyramid to the piece it touches: the icosahedra and the Unborns become two convex truncated octahedra that fill space. Main theorem. In the simple cubic lattice of regular icosahedra of edge 1 and spacing φ, the golden split of every AXE makes the icosahedron with its 12 pyramids, the Icosaxes , and the Unborn with its 12, the Unborn Axes , convex truncated octahedra with full octahedral symmetry, the same equiangular hexagon (sides 1/√2 and 1/(φ√2)), volumes 1 + 2√5/3 and 1 + √5/3, filling space face to face. Theorem 2: for any cut points inside the AXEs, both padded pieces are convex only if every AXE is cut at its golden point. Theorem 3: in the Lotus Jewel network the same cut gives the keyed pair Lotus Jewel Axes (volume √5) and Dodecaxes (volume 2), and every keying fills space. Theorem 4 (factor x): the pair belongs to a one-parameter family of mixed space-fillers, the truncated octahedra T(x) and T(1/x), from Kelvin's cell (x = 1) to the golden pair (x = τ). A remark places the octet (tetrahedra and octahedra) in a similar family between the rhombic dodecahedron and the cube. Exact in ℚ(√5). The two smooth shapes are known (Koca et al. 2015, x = τ and x = 1/τ); the route from the icosahedron lattice, the golden split and its uniqueness, and the keyed pair were not found in the sources checked. Paper #48 continues DICTO's search for mixed Platonic space-fillers (#47), answering his conjecture that a more elegant and simpler filling was within reach. The ideas and the names Unborn, AXE, Lotus Jewel, Icosaxes, Unborn Axes, Lotus Jewel Axes and Dodecaxes are DICTO's; computation, exact proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). title: The DICTO Ogdoecontahedron on the Octet Truss
description: Joined hexagon to hexagon, copies of the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron (OG) form a body-centred cubic packing whose gap is treated in a companion paper (DICTO DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23451210). Here the OG goes the other way: its eight joint hexagons lie exactly on the faces of a regular octahedron |x| + |y| + |z| = 2φ/3, so the OG sits in the octahedra of the octet truss, and the space round it becomes tractable. Exactly, in ℚ(√5), we give four families of space-filling kits. (1) A golden-key octet: the OG's golden envelope (a rhombic triacontahedron) pokes into each neighbouring tetrahedron as a small key whose base corners sit at the golden-section points of the octahedron's edges; keyed octahedron and dented tetrahedron (a left and a right) fill space. (2) A Penrose-core octet: the five-fold stars of neighbouring OGs face each other across every octahedron edge, offset by exactly one star tip radius, and an exact thick Penrose rhombus, with two φ-smaller ones, joins them; the shared middle piece holds three Penrose cores. (3) Golden envelopes on every octahedron never overlap and fill exactly 90 − 40√5 = 10/φ⁶ ≈ 55.73% of space; the rest is one chiral piece, so envelope and grown piece fill space with two shapes, and each envelope lies inside its rhombic dodecahedron touching all 12 faces at golden-section points. (4) One-piece glue: the rhombic dodecahedron round each octet vertex, or the octahedral cell round each edge midpoint, minus the OGs that bite it, fills space with the OG as two shapes with no mirror pair, the sockets being exact OG imprints; the edge-centred piece holds all three Penrose cores and can be keyed with the OG's own kites so that twelve copies lock round one OG. The main kits were proved exactly by an independent engine and checked with millions of sample points. Ideas, choices and names are DICTO's; computation, exact arithmetic and renders were done with Claude (Anthropic) as a research assistant; the independent exact proofs, the vertex glue W, the identification of the tetartoid and the keyed-glue design are by Claude Fable. title: The Polyhedral Stretching Theorem
description: In short. Take a regular dodecahedron and slide it one edge-length in a straight line. The shape it sweeps through has every edge the same length, whichever way you slide it, except when the slide runs exactly along one of its edges. Main theorem (the Polyhedral Stretching Theorem). Let P be a convex polyhedron whose edges all have length 1, and slide it a distance 1 along a direction u. The swept shape (the convex hull of P and P moved by u) has every edge of length 1 unless u is parallel to an edge of P. Its faces are: each face of P not parallel to u, kept whole; each n-sided face parallel to u, stretched into an (n+2)-gon, with one side fewer for each of its edges parallel to u; and one parallelogram for every edge of P's outline seen along u, a rhombus when the slide is 1. The proof is given in an appendix. For the dodecahedron: sliding along a cube axis gives DICTO's stretched dodecahedron (F11); along a five-fold axis the ten rhombi are all alike; along a face diagonal of Euclid's cube it gives the member DICTO found, all twelve pentagons and ten rhombi, which began as a void and two overlapping dodecahedra that DICTO saw in the dodecahedron layer of paper #47. Dodecahedra at the corners of a triangle or a tetrahedron give three- and four-cap forms with equilateral triangles among their faces. The theorem holds for every Platonic solid: the stretched icosahedra form a second new-looking family, and the tetrahedron and octahedron rediscover the cuboctahedron, the truncated tetrahedron and three Johnson solids. DICTO names the family the DICTO stretched solids: equal-edged when the stretch is one edge-length, telescoped at any other length. Attached: printable nets (five A4 nets with glue tabs) and DICTO's telescoping paper model, which slides from equal-edged to long, and the study with all scripts and checks. The stretched dodecahedron (F11), the long hexagon seen in the dodecahedron layer, the three- and four-cap forms and the telescoping model are DICTO's ideas; computation, proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). title: Every Mix of the Platonic Solids Fills Space
description: Main theorem. For every non-empty set M of the five Platonic solids, written D, I, C, T, O (dodecahedron, icosahedron, cube, tetrahedron, octahedron: the letters of DICTO), there is a tiling of space whose tiles are copies of the solids in M, all of edge 1, each solid of M used and no other Platonic solid of edge 1, together with copies of pieces from one kit of seven connectors: the half octahedron P, the tetrahedron's face pyramid Q, the same pyramid Q′ at size φ²/√2, DICTO's Admiral Caps A, the Dogstar S, and a cube of edge φ with one of Euclid's roofs taken away (X) or added (Y). Tiles need not meet face to face. The proof stacks flat slabs, one for each solid's world: dodecahedra and Dogstars on Euclid's cubes, edged with X and Y; cubes; the octet, edged with half octahedra; and icosahedra in Pacioli's position inside octahedra of edge φ²/√2, completed by the Admiral Caps. All 31 mixes are also spot-checked numerically. Corollaries: the cube alone and the tetrahedron with the octahedron need no connector, while every mix with the dodecahedron or the icosahedron, and the tetrahedron alone, the octahedron alone, cube + tetrahedron and cube + octahedron, need one; all five solids fill space together with six connectors; the six Admiral Caps of one icosahedron and one Dogstar have the same volume, φ/2. Open: whether cube + tetrahedron + octahedron need a connector, the smallest kit, the face-to-face version and three-way periodicity. Each result opens with a short explanation; figures show the seven pieces and the layer cake. The idea, to connect all the Platonic solids in any combination by building on the earlier work, is DICTO's; computation, proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). title: Aristotle's Pyramid
description: Main theorem. Of the five face pyramids of the Platonic solids (the cone from the centre over one face), a set fills space exactly when it is the cube's pyramid alone, the tetrahedron's and the octahedron's pyramids together, or the union of these two; no other set fills space. Here a set fills space when copies of its pyramids, in any numbers, any positions and mirror images, every kind used and not necessarily face to face, tile space. The proof is a Dehn-type counting map on dihedral angles, made rigorous with the Splitting Theorem of Conway, Radin and Sadun: the dodecahedron's and the icosahedron's pyramids can never occur, and the tetrahedron's occurs exactly when the octahedron's does; the octet truss cut from its centres and the cubic tiling give the tilings. Corollaries: alone only the cube's pyramid fills space, in pairs only the tetrahedron's with the octahedron's, and with equal edges their numbers are asymptotically equal; the icosahedron's pyramid, the Cleo-Icos (DICTO's name), fills space only with a partner that is not a face pyramid, Antonius (#20). The question is DICTO's: Aristotle wrote that among solids only "the pyramid and the cube" fill space (On the Heavens III.8); read as the regular tetrahedron this is false, and DICTO asked whether he could have meant the Cleo-Icos. A section after the theorem collects DICTO's earlier exact fillings by the whole Platonic solids with partners. Every angle identity, the test over all 31 sets and the constructions are checked in exact arithmetic. Finding #44 on dictospheres.com. title: The Reuleaux Platonic Solids
description: Main theorem. Put a ball on every corner of a Platonic solid of diameter 1, each of radius 1, and let B be what all the balls share (DICTO's idea). Then the smallest width of B is exactly 1, reached along any line through two corners at distance 1; and for the cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron, with circumradius ½ and inradius r, the width along each axis through a face centre is exactly 2√(3/4 + r²) − 2r. Corollary: dual solids have the same ratio r/R, so dual pairs have exactly the same face-axis width, (√30 − √3)/3 ≈ 1.248392 for the balls on the cube and on the octahedron and (√(50 + 2√5) − √(5 + 2√5))/√15 ≈ 1.110989 for the balls on the dodecahedron and on the icosahedron. The tetrahedron is the classical case, the Reuleaux tetrahedron, where the formula does not apply (its diameter is its edge, not twice its circumradius); its edge-midpoint axis gives √3 − √2/2 by the same argument, and our volume agrees with the known closed form to 1.1 × 10 −8 . The four other bodies (not found in the sources checked) are not Reuleaux polyhedra in the sense of Montejano and Roldán-Pensado, following Sallee, or of Hynd. Conjecture 1, with numerical evidence from 3000 directions and local refinement: these axes give the largest width. DICTO names the bodies by their look, the Reuleaux octahedron (balls on the cube), cube (on the octahedron), icosahedron (on the dodecahedron) and dodecahedron (on the icosahedron); each has the face pattern of the dual solid, and the fewest face colours are 4, 2, 3, 3 and 4. title: The DICTO Sunstar
description: Regular dodecahedra on alternate cubes of a cubic lattice (Euclid's dodecahedron: a cube with a roof on each face) are the densest lattice packing of the dodecahedron [9]; the hole left in each other cube is a star, the Dogstar , and dodecahedra and Dogstars fill space. The Dogstar and this tiling are Hart's [6]. We prove them exactly in ℚ(√5): the Dogstar is the cube minus the six roofs that reach into it, of volume exactly φ/2 at dodecahedron edge 1, and, as a stellation of the dodecahedron (Hart's), we identify it exactly: the dodecahedron 1/φ³ the size of the lattice's, with all 12 pyramids, 24 of the 30 wedges and 8 of the 20 spikes; it lies inside its own cube's stella octangula. The Star Chain Reaction : the great stellated dodecahedron of that core has the cell dodecahedron's 20 corners, and a whole Sunstar (a dodecahedron with the Dogstars on its six faces) 1/φ³ the size fits inside it exactly, with no room to grow, and so on for ever, ratio φ³. title: The DICTO Jewel
description: Put Euclid's dodecahedron on a cube, as roofs on its six faces, and carve away the stella octangulas of the six neighbouring cubes: what remains is the DICTO Jewel , with 38 corners and 60 faces, twelve of them thick Penrose rhombi (the windows) and 48 triangles, and volume exactly 3/16 at the scale where a 2 × 2 × 2 block of cells (the Hexa's cube, §4) has edge 1, or 12 on cells of edge 2. Jewels and stella octangulas on the other cells fill space in the rock-salt pattern, 3 : 1 by volume [2]; we prove this exactly: each stella's cube is the stella and six carved roofs of exactly 1/96 each. DICTO's clusters [2, 10], named here as single solids: the DICTO Jewel-Tetra (4 Jewels, 228 faces, 3/4), whose copies share out all Jewels, and the DICTO Jewel-Octa (6 Jewels and the stella that exactly fills their hole, 19/16), which tiles space with loose stellas (stellas inside no piece) on exactly 12 lattices of translations, all one tiling up to its symmetry. Together they sit in the pattern of the octet truss, eight Jewel-Tetras round each Jewel-Octa, but as overlapping solids, not as a tiling: without overlap at most one stella in six can be inside a Jewel-Octa, and the 12 lattices reach that bound. The third, the DICTO Jewel-Rhombi , is eight Jewels on the corners of the face-centred cubic cell, meeting on 18 windows, with the stella sealed inside (396 faces, 25/16). Each of the three tiles space with loose stellas (on 4, 12 and 25 lattices of translations; 2, 1 and 9 up to symmetry); none can without stellas, since Jewels are only three quarters of space. The DICTO Hexa and DICTO Hexa-Key [12] (5/4 and 3/4, filling space 5 : 3, two windows between neighbouring Hexas), checked numerically in [12], are proved exactly. As a solid the Jewel is pyritohedral, so it twins like the Ogdoecontahedron [5]; its packing does not twin by a (111) mirror, because that mirror does not keep the cube lattice. title: The DICTO Ogdoecontahedron on the Gyrated Octet
description: In a companion paper the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron (OG) sits in every octahedron of the octet truss, its eight joint hexagons on the eight faces. DICTO proposed that it can also live in the gyrated octet, the tetrahedral–octahedral honeycomb stacked A B A B, in which octahedron meets octahedron and tetrahedron meets tetrahedron across every layer. It can: the OGs on both sides of a layer meet on the same joint hexagon, but each is the mirror image of the other, and since the OG has no such mirror the layers are twin boundaries ; exactly, the twin is the OG turned 60° about the joint three-fold axis, the spinel law of crystallography. Cutting each octahedron into the OG and eight chiral caps, and keeping the tetrahedra whole, gives one exact kit for the octet, the gyrated octet and every stacking between ; at a twin layer a left and a right cap join into a twin cap and two tetrahedra into a triangular bipyramid. The facing-star middle piece of the octet fails at twin layers, and a mirror middle piece of volume (424 − 88√5)/4617 takes its place; with one boundary cap and one boundary tetrahedron the octet's Penrose-core kit then fills the gyrated octet and a single twin layer exactly, and with the same pieces any stacking; its Penrose cores lie only on the edges within the layers. The trait runs in the family: the OCD Stella twins in the same way, meeting its twin on a whole joint triangle; the golden envelope does not fit as it is, but cut flat at two opposite three-fold corners it becomes a solid of its own, the DICTO Belted Triacontahedron (DBT) , which fills the gyrated octet's octahedra pole to pole without overlap, 55.02% of space. Cut the same way at all eight of the corners that point through the octahedron's faces, it becomes the DICTO Octahedrally Truncated Triacontahedron (DICTO OTT) , with the OG's own symmetry, which twins like the OG, lies inside its octahedron and so fits every stacking, 52.89% of space. For each, the rest of space is filled by one more shape (two hands of one in the octet): the DICTO Fill sets . The DICTO Jewel's packing, framed by cubes, does not continue across a twin layer. All claims are exact in ℚ(√5) except where marked float. Companion to The DICTO Ogdoecontahedron on the Octet Truss (#37), DICTO DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23457016. Finding #37a on dictospheres.com. title: The DICTO OG Family on Every Stacking
description: One exact kit of pieces builds the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron (OG) into the octet, the gyrated octet, the classical polytypes between them and a Fibonacci crystal that never repeats; the OG family stacks like a real mineral, twinning by the spinel law. Two short rules say why. The tetrahedral–octahedral honeycomb falls into layers, and each layer can be laid on the one below in two ways: as in the octet truss (c) or as its mirror image in the shared plane (h). Any word in c and h is a stacking, exactly as for close-packed crystals, whose polytypes 3C, 2H, 4H, 6H, 9R, 15R … are words of this kind. The OG sits exactly in the octahedra of the octet [2] and of the gyrated octet [3]; here we place it, and the solids of its family, in every stacking. The twin rule : if a solid is centrosymmetric and has a three-fold axis at right angles to the layers, its mirror image in a layer plane is the same solid turned 60° about that axis; unless it also has a mirror at right angles to the axis, this is a true twin. The fit rule : a solid that lies in its own layer and does not overlap its copies within the layer fits every stacking, whatever the word. The OG, the DICTO OTT and the OCD Stella lie in their octahedra, and [3] showed that they fit every stacking; the rules explain why. The DICTO Belted Triacontahedron (DBT) leaves its octahedron but not its layer, so it too fits every stacking (shown in [3] only for the gyrated octet); exactly in ℚ(√5), the golden envelope (a rhombic triacontahedron) it was cut from fits the octet but overlaps at every h plane by exactly the volume of the two tips the DBT removes. The shares of space do not depend on the stacking: OG 1025/114 − 145√5/38 ≈ 45.89%, OTT 176/3 − 26√5 ≈ 52.89%, DBT 493/6 − 73√5/2 ≈ 55.02%. For the OG we give the kit per cell for 3C, 2H, 4H, 6H, 9R and 15R, and for the Fibonacci stacking (c → ch, h → c), which never repeats: in the limit exactly (3 − √5)/2 of the planes between layers are h planes (twin planes), and a cell needs 5 + √5 caps, (3 − √5)/2 twin caps, √5 − 1 tetrahedra and (3 − √5)/2 bipyramids, all exact. title: Universal PiTet: The DICTO PiTet Proposition
description: DICTO specified a five-fold version of the octet: spherical shells grown outward from the Cleo star, the same pattern each time with different solids, triangles and pyramids staying constant (hence the name PiTet: Pi for the spherical progression, Tet for the triangles). We give a rule that does this and prove, in exact arithmetic in ℚ(√5), what it produces. Let T take a convex solid with corners v to the solid {x : v·x ≤ v·v for every corner v}: each new face passes through a corner of the last solid at right angles to it. Starting from the icosidodecahedron (ID), T gives the rhombic triacontahedron (RT), then the DICTO GTI (Golden Truncated Icosahedron: hexagon sides 1 : φ), then the DICTO FPD (Flat Pentakis Dodecahedron), and then the ID again, exactly 10/φ⁴ = 35 − 15√5 times larger; the cycle therefore repeats without end. Each solid lies in the next, each shell is filled by congruent pieces of one or two kinds (exact volumes), and the whole chain is its own polar about the GTI's circumsphere. Below the cycle, the Cleo star (82 pieces) and 12 twisted frusta (Monkey Staff B) close the ID; the pieces on one five-fold axis join into a convex five-sided Vajra, and the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron fits between the ID and the RT with 20 pure hexagonal Cleos. Every claim is checked exactly. More of DICTO's geometry: https://dictospheres.com View in the app: https://kaleidohedra.dictospheres.com/?open=up

title: The DICTO OG Family: Four Steps Up and Four Down
description: In Universal PiTet a single rule T builds each solid from the last: every corner v of a solid S gives the face plane v·x = v·v, through v and at right angles to the line from the centre, and T(S) is the solid these planes bound. Started at the icosidodecahedron it closes into a four-step cycle. DICTO proposed running it from the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron (OG), and also running it the other way. The reverse step P takes as new corners the foot points of S's face planes, the points of those planes nearest the centre. From the OG, four steps of T give four solids with 92, 180, 212 and 270 corners, the DICTO KRE, PHE, TPP and DPHP , and four steps of P give four with 80, 132, 140 and 162 corners, the DICTO TPH, TQH, TQP and TQHD . All eight are proved exactly in ℚ(√5), each with the full icosahedral symmetry, and each step of P is undone exactly by T. Several have regular faces: 12 regular pentagons (PHE, TPH, TQP), 20 regular hexagons (PHE, DPHP, TQH, TQHD); the KRE has 30 rhombi and 60 kites. The family does not cycle. It nests as shells for three steps up, OG ⊂ KRE ⊂ PHE ⊂ TPP, and two steps down, TQH ⊂ TPH ⊂ OG, and each of these shells, and also the shell TQHD ⊂ TQP, is filled exactly by one piece per face of the inner solid. Both directions then break in the same way: 60 corners of the TPP stand outside the DPHP, and 60 corners of the TQP outside the TQH. In the plane, T and P are the classical antipedal and pedal constructions; the polyhedral pedal construction was posed as an open problem in 2010. We found the eight solids in no source. title: A Fibonacci Spine in a Five-fold Chorus of Ogdoecontahedron Packings
description: The DICTO Ogdoecontahedron is a convex, centrally symmetric icosahedral solid with 20 regular hexagons and 60 kites. Its hexagon directions contain five inscribed cubes, and each cube gives a periodic (body-centred cubic) packing in which copies meet face to face on hexagons. We place the five packings ("voices") in five 72° wedges round a five-fold axis, which is the icosahedral irrational twin, and remove clashing copies in whole five-fold rings. Checked exactly in ℚ(√5), the result is overlap-free to radius 10 (2756 sites, 385 removed, 7465 close pairs). Every copy lies at a golden height (m + nφ)u along the axis. Apart from one ring, the removed copies nearest the axis lie in one plane on a rank-2 lattice with axis slope −φ; together with the central copy, which is kept, they are exactly the points of the canonical singular Fibonacci cut-and-project chain with window [0, W), W² = 64/81 + 128√5/405. The window has a mechanism: a ring of five plane copies overlaps itself exactly when it is closer to the axis than t c , t c ² = 8/9 + 8√5/45. Since t c < W and no plane lattice point lies between them for |h| < 12.81, the two windows select the same points there. At h = 12.81 the core copy overlaps one other copy, which overlaps two more; on finite patches (integer program, float clash test) keeping the core copy is cheaper by one ring, here and at the next three such points. Minimal removal therefore thins the spine to a three-gap chain beyond |h| = 12.81, and staying pure Fibonacci costs at least one extra ring at each such point. Thus aperiodic order appears where periodic packings meet: the lattice of the chain is a plane section of one packing, its internal coordinate is the distance from the axis, and its window is fixed by the ring clash at t c . Irrational interfaces as one-dimensional quasicrystals, model sets near irrational lines and hard-core windows are known; we did not find this selection along a five-fold junction line, its self-clash window or the departure from it, and present them as a new exact instance of known ideas. Version 2 adds a discussion of the chain as a link between periodic and aperiodic order (abstract, §1, §9), checked for overstatement by an independent review; the results are unchanged from Version 1. title: Theaetetus: an icosahedron held exactly by its Cleo-Icos, grown to the DICTO Hecatodihedron in two exact stories
description: We hollow the DICTO-ICOSA star (the DICTO-Star with a pyramid on each of its 152 free faces) and find that a core icosahedron resting on twelve inner tips is loose: it turns about 14° before it touches anything. DICTO's remedy is to hold it with Cleo-Icos (an icosahedron's face pyramids from its centre) standing on the twenty triangles of the icosidodecahedron of edge 1, points inward. Their points land exactly on the face centres of an icosahedron of edge 1 , the same edge as every other piece, because the icosidodecahedron's triangles lie at twice that icosahedron's inradius; held so, the core cannot turn or shift. The hollow is then exactly the core, twelve flat pentagonal pyramids ( Aetos ) and twenty triangular antiprisms (the shadow of Klitzing's four-dimensional segmentochoron K-4.137), each antiprism a Cleo-Ico, three Sphen and three Sphenion , with volumes Cleo-Ico : Sphen : Sphenion = 3 : 2 : 1 and each Aetos exactly √5 Cleo-Icos. Grown outward with the layers of the Spheres of Dharma (scaled by 2/φ), the object closes on the DICTO Hecatodihedron (102 faces) in two exact stories. In the stations (215 pieces) every layer is a closed solid, each Cleo-Ico fused with the dodecahedron's corner pyramid into an Atraktos . In the 102 clean pieces , none with a dent, the core is cut into its twenty Cleo-Icos and the dodecahedron round it into twenty Kion by the same twenty cones from the centre, so the dual pair of icosahedron and dodecahedron is cut face to corner. Every volume is exact in ℚ(√5) and both stories sum to the Hecatodihedron, 3350 − 1486√5, with no remainder. The object is the Theaetetus world of the Kaleidohedra app. Data, renders and the check outputs are included. title: Progenitors
description: The DICTO Hecatodihedron H (102 faces) and its polar, the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron O (80 faces), came out of the Spheres of Dharma, an exact cycle of icosahedral shells that repeats every φ³. DICTO proposed that the twin pair could seed a cycle of its own. Every solid here is exact in ℚ(√5), and every nesting and volume is checked with remainder 0. On their own the twins do not close golden. H, O and their classical relatives, nested tightly in every order (8,742 cycles), never return on a power of φ, and the tightest 3-cycle gains exactly 9/φ⁴ = (3/φ²)² per round: a cycle governed by 3, as in Double Vision . The cycle then holds the core and hull of two dual compounds, the icosahedron–dodecahedron compound (ID, RT) and the twins' own compound, the DICTO Hecatogdoecontahedron (rTI, jtI). title: The DICTO Ogdoecontahedron
description: DICTO proposed turning the Spheres of Dharma, an exact endless nesting of six icosahedral solids, inside out. We include the cycle's in-between stage, the DICTO Truncated-Icosahedral Hecatodihedron, as a seventh station and take every station's polar reciprocal: the nesting reverses, and every station becomes a classical solid except one. The polar of the Hecatodihedron is new, and DICTO named it the Ogdoecontahedron for its 80 faces. It has 20 regular hexagons and 60 kites, 102 corners and 180 edges, only two edge lengths and two dihedral angles, no insphere and no midsphere, and 90 of its corners on one sphere, the inside-out image of the Hecatodihedron's 90 faces touching one sphere; every coordinate is exact in ℚ(√5). It is the pentakis dodecahedron with its 20 six-fold corners cut off flat. In the reversed cycle its 90 sphere corners lie on the icosidodecahedron's sphere, its hexagons hold the icosidodecahedron's triangles and its kites lie in the pentakis dodecahedron's faces. Its face arrangement is known (the dual of L0 applied to the dodecahedron, in the notation of the Antiprism software), but the metric solid was not found in the sources checked. Copies joined face to face on hexagons form a diamond network whose joints lie on a pyrochlore lattice; two such networks together are a body-centred cubic packing filling exactly (9225 − 3915√5)/608 ≈ 77.43% of space. It is neither a patch nor a cluster of the canonical (primitive) icosahedral quasicrystal; five of its periodic packings meeting round a five-fold axis are the subject of a separate paper (#30). Data, scripts and exact check outputs are included (see README.md); the full studies are at https://github.com/DICTOR-Master/kaleidohedra (branch research: studies/2026-10-16-polar-dharma, studies/2026-10-16-ocd-pyrochlore, studies/2026-10-16-ogdoecontahedron-bridge). title: Golden Bodhi Pyrochlore
description: Copies of the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron joined face to face on their hexagons form a body-centred cubic packing that fills (9225 − 3915√5)/608 ≈ 77.43% of space (DICTO DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23404688). This paper is about the remaining 22.57%. Exactly, in ℚ(√5): each copy's share of the gap is its Voronoi cell, a truncated octahedron, minus the solid, and cones from the centre over the 72 free faces cut it into 72 convex pieces of 3 kinds whose volumes add up with remainder 0. Asking what could fill the gap more naturally, DICTO proposed partners, bridges, hexagonal limbs and adapters. The limbs are tilted hexagonal prisms, one per free hexagon, which cross in pairs at the centres of the cell's square faces; their crossing zone has exactly two golden-rhombus faces, the faces of the rhombic triacontahedron and the golden rhombohedra. From there a golden fill suggests itself: golden rhombohedra, DICTO's Cleo-Icos as adapters from hexagons to golden planes, and the Bodhi pieces, which are all bounded by golden-rhombus planes. Each copy's golden envelope is a rhombic triacontahedron; cut at the joints, the envelopes divide the packing into 77.4% solid, 11.8% non-golden shell and 10.7% golden region. But the golden region does not divide naturally into Bodhi pieces: cut canonically by every golden plane, even in DICTO's five-fold chorus arrangement, it shatters into 8,027 pieces (exact), with only five Bodhi pieces among them. So we ask what any golden fill must contain. Exactly: the golden region's walls are golden planes except for 24 small star-tip triangles per cell, which lie in the three-fold joint planes and meet the neighbouring golden faces at 20.905° (cos² = φ²/3), so golden rhombohedra and Bodhi pieces alone can never fill it. One adapter removes the obstruction: the GBPC (Golden Bodhi Pyrochlore Corner), a low triangular pyramid shaped like the rhombic triacontahedron's three-fold corner and the golden conjugate of DICTO's Cleo-Ico, 24 per cell, overlapping nothing. What remains has only golden walls and five-fold edges, and no local obstruction is left. But it has no face-to-face tiling by golden rhombohedra: for one size, its walls fix the edge at a rational multiple of φ and a Galois-conjugate count then demands a negative number of oblate rhombohedra (exact; the counting step checked independently); and a face-to-face tiling cannot mix sizes. Whether it tiles other than face to face is open; random and symmetric searches fill at most 66.9% of it, and flat slabs between second neighbours need golden layers of sizes our searches did not use. DICTO's own answer to the gap is not golden but whole: cut point by point at the octahedral holes of the bcc lattice, three per copy, each between six copies, the gap falls into identical pieces, the Bull-horns OG adaptor, partly golden-faced, each exactly one third of a copy's gap, (18728 − 6296√5)/41553 ≈ 0.111898 or 7.5223% of space; copies and adaptors fill space exactly with two shapes. Float explorations are labelled as such. More of DICTO's geometry: https://dictospheres.com View in the app: https://kaleidohedra.dictospheres.com/?open=bodhiPyro

title: Inverted Shells: The Spheres of Dharma Turned Inside Out
description: The Spheres of Dharma nest six icosahedral solids exactly, from an icosahedron out to the icosahedron φ³ larger; between the truncated icosahedron and the triacontahedron, the layer closes part-way into the DICTO Hecatodihedron. DICTO proposed turning the cycle inside out. Turning each layer's pieces over does not work: no layer closes into a shell. Taking the six solids and the Hecatodihedron stage as seven stations and replacing each by its polar reciprocal reverses the nesting and gives a new exact cycle: dodecahedron ⊂ icosidodecahedron ⊂ Ogdoecontahedron ⊂ pentakis dodecahedron ⊂ icosahedron ⊂ rhombic triacontahedron ⊂ dodecahedron φ³ larger (volume ratio φ⁹). Its one new station, the dual of the Hecatodihedron, is the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron (DICTO DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23404688). Cutting each layer by cones over the faces of its inner solid gives one kind of piece per layer (12, 12, 20, 60, 20, 30), every volume exact in ℚ(√5) with remainder 0. The cycle inherits two loose ends. Tightening them gives an evenly stepped nest, still one kind per layer and exact. Left loose, the large outer gap holds the great stellated dodecahedron at exactly one size: its 20 points on the outer dodecahedron's corners, its 12 valleys on the triacontahedron's tips, cutting the gap into 60 tetrahedra and 60 pentagonal pyramids. The inner gap admits no star and no locked dual pair among those tested, but the truncated icosidodecahedron pair fits in reverse order (as polarity demands), with play exactly √5·φ³/9. The golden rectangles that frame the whole are the outer dodecahedron's own small stellation, and the cycle repeats inward without end. We also record the checks this study forced on us, because three of our first tables were wrong. Data, scripts and exact check outputs are included (see README.md); the full studies are at https://github.com/DICTOR-Master/kaleidohedra (branch research: studies/2026-10-16-polar-dharma, studies/2026-10-16-flip-test, studies/_lib). Computation, exact arithmetic and checking with Claude (Anthropic); an independent pre-publication check by Claude Fable. Explore DICTO's worlds in the apps: https://dictospheres.com Version 2. Version 2 corrects one sentence: the Ogdoecontahedron is not called a new solid; it is the canonical pentakis dodecahedron cut at the hexagon planes, an unnamed solid derived from a known one (see the Hecatodihedron paper, Version 2, DICTO DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23360857). title: Double Vision – Both Cycles in One Space
description: The Spheres of Dharma nest six icosahedral solids, with the Hecatodihedron as an in-between stage; their polar reciprocal is a second exact cycle in which every nesting is reversed (Inverted Shells). We put both cycles in one space. The sphere of reciprocation is then the one free choice, and polarity with the cycle's φ³ repeat gives mirror spheres every φ 3/2 in radius. At ρ² = φ²/4 the two cycles share the icosahedron and dodecahedron; at ρ² = 3φ²/4 they share the icosidodecahedron and triacontahedron; no sphere gives both, because the two settings differ by a factor 3, which is not a power of φ, and the loose ends of the cycle cannot be bent far enough to close the gap. Cutting every piece of one cycle by every piece of the other gives one solid of convex pieces, exact in ℚ(√5) with remainder 0 in every piece and layer: per turn, 536 pieces of 12 kinds in the first setting and 502 pieces of 11 kinds in the second. The setting moves where the two cycles cut each other: the first cuts the outer roofs hardest and leaves the dodecahedron columns whole; the second leaves the roofs, pyramids and tetrahedra whole and cuts the columns. The innermost layer is cut in both. Data, scripts and exact check outputs are included (see README.md); the full studies are at https://github.com/DICTOR-Master/kaleidohedra (branch research: studies/2026-10-16-interlock, studies/2026-10-16-polar-dharma, studies/_lib). title: The FUJI Family: Pyramids on Flat-Ended Triangles
description: FUJI is the hexagonal pyramid that closes the corners of our thirteen-icosahedron cluster, the Lotus seed [1]. Its base is a flat-ended triangle : a hexagon with all angles 120° and sides 1 and 1/φ alternating. The same shape kept turning up elsewhere, in our cuboctahedral PET-bottle spheres and in the colouring of the Lotus seed, so we asked whether FUJI belongs to a family. It does. Put an apex over a flat-ended triangle with sides 1 and r, with all six side edges of length 1. This gives a one-parameter family FUJI(r) , running from the regular tetrahedron (r = 0) through FUJI (r = 1/φ) to the flat regular hexagon (r = 1). We derive the base angles and prove: The base angles (derived): cos L = (1 + 2r)/3 and cos² S = (2 + r)/(3(2 − r)). The antiprism rule: the member whose base continues the plane of the n-gonal antiprism's triangles is r = 2 cos(π/n) − 1 , so that 1 + r is the short diagonal of the regular n-gon (for n = 3, its side). The wheel bound: flat wheels crossing along different spokes number at most 3 (square), 4 (hexagonal) or 6 (decagonal), and five octagonal wheels are impossible. The octahedron gives the tetrahedron, the square antiprism √2 − 1, and the pentagonal antiprism (the middle of the icosahedron) gives FUJI. The members turn up in several places: The golden hexagon of a construction after Odom is FUJI's base; the same construction with any extension gives every member with r < 1. The space-filling truncated tetrahedron of Damasceno, Engel and Glotzer has the r = 1/2 member's base as its faces. In a breathing pyrochlore the kagome hexagons are flat-ended triangles, with r equal to the breathing ratio; as a Wythoff construction it tiles space for every r. The equal-depth cube–octahedron solid has the cuboctahedral member's base, r = (√3 − 1)/2, as its eight triangles, and its cube corners are exactly that member's apexes; we prove the two conditions are the same. Cleo-Icos and Antonius: the icosahedron's central pyramid is the corner of the prolate golden rhombohedron, which splits into Cleo-Icos + Antonius + Cleo-Icos; so the two fill space, two to one, and build the rhombic hexecontahedron. DICTO · dictospheres.com. Computation, checking and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). Data, scripts, proofs and checks: studies/2026-10-14-fuji-family in https://github.com/DICTOR-Master/kaleidohedra. Version 2 adds Figure 11: Pacioli's golden rectangles and the 20 Cleo-Icos. Version 3 credits the Cleo-Icos as the unit tetrahedron of the Mackay icosahedron (Mackay 1962; Ino 1969; Marks 1984; Kabai 2014) and the golden rhombohedron as a distorted fcc cell (Prodan et al. 2017). Version 4 (2026-10-14): the Cleo-Icos in classical geometry, as the twin of the dodecahedron's central pyramid in Hypsicles' "Book XIV" of Euclid (c. 150 BC); the golden-hexagon construction credited to Sándor Kabai's Wolfram Demonstration "Hexagons and the Golden Ratio" (2008). No other changes. View in the app: https://kaleidohedra.dictospheres.com/?open=breathing

title: AXE, CLEO and FUJI: the Gap Pieces of the Icosahedron
description: Abstract. Regular icosahedra cannot fill space: two of them sharing an edge leave 83.62° around it. Our thirteen-icosahedron cluster, the Lotus seed , closes every gap with three small pieces, AXE , CLEO and FUJI . With whole icosahedra they fill an icosahedron of edge φ² exactly, in 113 pieces, or in 63 pieces as we first built it: a dodecahedron, 12 J11, 30 AXE and 20 FUJI. AXE and CLEO are two of the Mosseri–Sadoc tiles, scaled by 1/τ; here they arise as the gap pieces of a cluster of whole icosahedra. FUJI, a hexagonal pyramid, is new. It is not a union of Mosseri–Sadoc tiles at its own scale or larger (proofs by the Dehn invariant and by the angles of its base). The three pieces recur throughout our work: the Dodecahedral Chain (great stellated and excavated dodecahedra), the dodecahedron as a small icosahedron with 12 caps, 30 AXE and 20 CLEO, the Chain of Karma at every scale, and the Stella-Corona network. The names are ours: AXE is shaped like an axe head; CLEO is named after Cleopatra's Needle in London; FUJI has the shape of Mount Fuji and the colour of the fuji flower, Japanese wisteria. Every volume, angle and count is recomputed from the study data (CHECKS.json). Printable A4 nets are included, so the Lotus seed can be built by hand. title: Capturing the In-betweens: a Study of Transitional Polyhedral Shells
description: Our Chain of Karma, Spheres of Dharma and Bodhi Seed are exact icosahedral dissections: each grows a large polyhedron from a small core by adding rings of congruent pieces. Between the familiar solids at the start and end of each step lie the in-between stages, the transitional shells . Taking each stage as one solid, with its pieces fused, the builds pass through celebrated polyhedra on the way: Icosahedron + 20 CLEO is Kepler's great stellated dodecahedron. Adding 30 AXE turns it into the excavated dodecahedron , a stellation of the icosahedron, with all 32 corners kept. Adding 12 caps closes the dodecahedron : the Dodecahedral Chain walks from the icosahedron to its dual through two star solids. The Bodhi Seed's centre + 60 Vajra (fine) is the rhombic hexecontahedron. The Spheres of Dharma's seventh stage is a convex solid with 102 faces and 80 corners : 12 regular pentagons, 30 rhombi and 60 triangles, its rhombi and triangles tangent to one sphere. Not found in the catalogues we searched, we name it the DICTO Truncated-Icosahedral Hecatodihedron . Every identification is checked against an independent construction to within 10⁻⁴. The paper describes all 21 piece types (with their names, including Stupa and Monkey Staff), shows 45 further convex stages, and gives cut-out nets so the in-betweens can be built by hand. The transitional shells have their own group, DICTO Transitional Shells, in the Polyhedraverse app. Files: the paper (PDF), cut-out nets for four shells (A4 PDF), and the data, scripts, figures and checks (zip). Computation and checking were done with Claude (Anthropic) in the open-source library krp-core. Version 3 corrects Section 4.6: only the 30 rhombi and 60 triangles of the DICTO Truncated-Icosahedral Hecatodihedron touch one sphere (radius 1.5); its 12 pentagons lie at 1.4384, so it has no insphere. Version 2 said all 102 faces were tangent. View in the app: https://kaleidohedra.dictospheres.com/?open=chains:dharma

title: The DICTO Truncated-Icosahedral Hecatodihedron
description: We describe a convex polyhedron with 102 faces, 80 corners and 180 edges that arises as the seventh stage of our Spheres of Dharma, a cycle of nested icosahedral shells. It is the truncated icosahedron with a low hexagonal pyramid (a Shield ) on each of its 20 hexagons, at the one height at which the two triangles of neighbouring Shields across every hexagon–hexagon edge lie in a single plane. Its faces are 12 regular pentagons, 30 rhombi and 60 isosceles triangles; it has only two edge angles. Combinatorially it is Conway's hexakis truncated icosahedron k6tI (132 faces) with its 60 coplanar triangle pairs merged into 30 rhombi. The rhombi and triangles all touch one sphere; the pentagons lie a little inside it, so the solid has no insphere. We name it the DICTO Truncated-Icosahedral Hecatodihedron ( hecatodi- , one hundred and two). This corrects an earlier statement of ours that all 102 faces touch one sphere. DICTO · dictospheres.com. Computation and checking with Claude (Anthropic). Discovery #28 in DISCOVERIES.md of https://github.com/DICTOR-Master/kaleidohedra. Version 2. Version 2 corrects "60 pairs" to 30, and adds an exact relation found in a prior-art search: the Hecatodihedron's 20 Shield apices are the canonical pentakis dodecahedron's three-fold vertices, so it is the joined truncated icosahedron (jtI) with its 12 five-fold corners cut off at the pentagon planes, an unnamed solid derived from a known one; and the DICTO Hecatogdoecontahedron, its self-dual compound with the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron (182 faces), whose core and hull are those of the classical truncated icosahedron–pentakis dodecahedron compound. title: DICTO ATOM-13×13: thirteen clusters of thirteen, twelve around one, six golden and seven periodic, with the pieces that fill between them
description: Twelve equal spheres can touch a thirteenth and no more (Schütte and van der Waerden 1952), and twelve atoms round one make the icosahedral cluster of liquids and metals (Frank 1952). We set thirteen polyhedral thirteens side by side, each a centre and twelve around it. Six are golden, on the icosahedron's five-fold axes: the Icosa-13 (Lotus seed), DESHI, the Dodeca-13, UNITY with its closed form VENUS, the DICTO-Star and the Bodhi seed. Seven are periodic, a cell and twelve neighbours in a honeycomb: the rhombic dodecahedron (RD 13, with its rounded form the DICTO Spheroid-13 RD), our skewed RD, the Bain RD, the golden Bilinski dodecahedron, the regular-hexagon elongated dodecahedron, the truncated octahedron (4 + 5 + 4, the centre seen through two square windows) and the DICTO Jewel (with its stella octangulas). For each we give how the twelve touch the centre and one another, and the kits that fill between them: 24 kits from 13 to 213 pieces, every one checked piece by piece and buildable from the centre out. Two golden clusters close exactly into a φ²-times larger copy of their own form. Every periodic block fills space by translation alone, and all seven are the same tiling in different shapes: under a linear change of coordinates each neighbourhood is the face-centred cubic one, whose radius-one perfect code is known (Kovačević and Tan 2018; explicitly x₁ + 3x₂ + 9x₃ ≡ 0 mod 13, Kovačević 2026), its weights Singer's difference set {0, 1, 3, 9} mod 13 (Singer 1938). Credit: the clusters and their names (Lotus seed, DESHI, UNITY, VENUS, DICTO-Star, Bodhi seed, DICTO Spheroid-13 RD, the DICTO Jewel, the truncated octahedron's 4 + 5 + 4 with its two square windows, the piece names, DICTO ATOM-13×13), the choice of members and the gold centre are DICTO's. Computation and checking with Claude (Anthropic). Files: the paper (PDF), and a data archive with every cluster and kit as pieces, the 24 kit plans for the Polyhedraverse app, the facts table, renders and scripts. title: DICTO Spheroid-13 RD: a true rhombic dodecahedron wrapped by twelve keyed pieces, a nearly round block of thirteen that fills space by translation alone
description: A rhombic dodecahedron with its twelve face neighbours, thirteen cells of the face-centred cubic (FCC) honeycomb, fills space by translation alone: of the 183 sublattices of index 13 in the FCC lattice, exactly 8 have the thirteen lattice points as a complete set of representatives, and the 8 are turns of one arrangement, with block translations of length √10 (neighbour spacing √2). Keeping that tiling, we reshape the block: the centre stays a true rhombic dodecahedron, only larger, and the twelve cells around it are moved, corner class by corner class and the same in every block, with every face flat and every cell convex with a minimum thickness, to make the block's outer surface as small as possible. The result, the DICTO Spheroid-13 RD, is nearly round while its outside stays keyed: at minimum thickness 0.15 its roundness 36πV²/S³ is 0.707 (the plain block 0.365, a single rhombic dodecahedron 0.741, and the block lattice's Voronoi cell, the roundest single tile with these translations, 0.748), with a centre 1.525 times the size of the lattice's own cells. The block has the tiling's full symmetry (order 6), so it uses three piece shapes: the centre and two outer kinds of six, each three pieces and their mirror images. Each block meets 14 others across all 84 of its outer faces; the centres never meet. Four thicknesses are given (0.08 to 0.35), with printable nets at one scale per set; as a variant, the centre left free to reshape gains at most 0.01 in roundness. The block tiling itself is known: it is the radius-one perfect code of the A₃ lattice (Kovačević and Tan 2018), written explicitly as x₁ + 3x₂ + 9x₃ ≡ 0 (mod 13) by Kovačević (2026), and its weights 0, 1, 3, 9 are Singer's perfect difference set of the projective plane of order 3. What is new here is the block as thirteen rhombic dodecahedra, rounded and keyed around a true rhombic dodecahedron, with its pieces and nets. Credit: the question whether the rhombic dodecahedron's thirteen fills space as the DICTO Hexa does, the rounded, keyed quality of the block, the true rhombic dodecahedron at its centre, the choice of thicknesses and the name DICTO Spheroid-13 RD are DICTO's. Computation and checking with Claude (Anthropic). Files: the paper (PDF), and a data archive with the scripts, all results, 15 printable A4 nets (one scale per set) and renders. Version 2 (2026-10-14): the paper is written in the first person throughout; no other changes. title: Spheres of Dharma: a second endless golden cycle of the icosahedral solids, through the icosidodecahedron, the fullerene cage and the rhombic triacontahedron
description: We describe an exact, endlessly repeating nesting of six icosahedral solids (the Ritsudō cycle), each layer filled by a few repeated pieces. With the dodecahedron at edge 1: an icosahedron of edge 1/φ, an icosidodecahedron of edge φ/2 (around it 12 pentagonal pyramids and 20 twisted triangular frusta), the dodecahedron (20 triangular pyramids), a truncated icosahedron of edge 1/φ, the fullerene cage (12 twisted pentagonal frusta and 30 Mosseri–Sadoc tetrahedra t1 at scale 1/φ), a rhombic triacontahedron of edge ½√(45 − 18√5) = 1.089814 (12 pentagonal and 20 hexagonal caps and 60 tetrahedral wedges), and an icosahedron of edge φ² (30 edge and 20 face pieces). The outer icosahedron is φ³ times the inner one, so the cycle repeats without end in both directions; one cycle has 237 pieces. All pieces of a cycle are checked to be free of overlap, with total volume exact. The construction rests on three exact relations: the icosahedron and the dodecahedron share the icosidodecahedron as their core, differing only in 12 pentagonal or 20 triangular corner pyramids; the fullerene cage wraps the dodecahedron at exactly one golden step, the dodecahedron's corners on the cage's hexagon centres; and the rhombic triacontahedron is the cage, with its 60 corners on the triacontahedron's faces, plus caps and wedges. The cycle shares its dodecahedron and its two icosahedra with the Lotus seed of the Chain of Karma, and each half of either structure fills its side of that dodecahedron exactly, so the two can be exchanged half by half at every scale. The cycle grows concentrically, one icosahedron per cycle (Nenrin growth), while the Lotus seed branches, 13 icosahedra per φ² step; the Lotus seed's 12 corner icosahedra straddle the shared dodecahedron, so they stay whole only when both halves are the Lotus seed's. The five cubes of the dodecahedron lie in the network's seams, and the five octahedra on the icosidodecahedron hold one icosahedron of edge 1 in Pacioli's golden position. Its outer shell, the rhombic triacontahedron, is the only other form found to branch like the Lotus seed (the Bodhi seed, described separately). The shells are the family of the Tsai-type cluster of icosahedral quasicrystals, here solid and exactly filled. Checks. All 237 pieces of one cycle are pairwise free of overlap (separating axes), lie inside the outer icosahedron, and their total volume equals I(φ²) to 1e-12. The triacontahedron's edge is exactly ½√(45 − 18√5) = 1.0898138. Terms: Ritsudō (律動, rhythm) for the six-shell cycle; Nenrin (年輪, tree rings) for its concentric growth. The icosidodecahedron as the twin form, the dual triangular structures, the triangles of rhombi, the fullerene transition, the last missing layer and all names are DICTO's. Computation and checking were done with Claude (Anthropic). Files: the paper (PDF) and its data, scripts, logs and renders (zip; also at https://github.com/DICTOR-Master/kaleidohedra). title: Vajrayana
description: Progenitors (DICTO DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23413184) set the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron O into the Spheres of Dharma in the dodecahedron's place and found an exact nine-station golden cycle, I ⊂ ID ⊂ O ⊂ rTI ⊂ TI ⊂ H ⊂ jtI ⊂ RT ⊂ I·φ³, closing on φ⁹ in volume. This companion asks where the dodecahedron went and what fills the cycle's loose steps. Every solid here is exact in ℚ(√5), and every nesting and volume is checked with remainder 0 unless marked float. The dodecahedron returns inside the icosidodecahedron, as the hull of DICTO's Cleo star: the icosahedron's 20 Cleo-Icos with 20 more turned outward have their tips exactly at (2/3)·D, and 82 pieces of four kinds fill that dodecahedron exactly. The loose step from the rhombic triacontahedron to the next icosahedron is closed by the DICTO Metaxyhexecontahedron: the member of the dodecahedron–icosahedron hull family whose icosahedron edge is 9/φ⁴ times its dodecahedron edge. It touches both neighbours, both of its layers are a single kind of piece, and its dual closes the same step in the polar-reversed cycle. The full-height icosidodecahedron star gives a second member of the same family, the DICTO Palintriacontahedron, the rhombic triacontahedron turned inside out. The cycle grows to twelve stations; the loose step O ⊂ rTI stays open. Prior-art status is stated claim by claim in §5. Data, scripts and exact check outputs are included (see README.md); the full study is at https://github.com/DICTOR-Master/kaleidohedra (branch research: studies/2026-10-16-progenitors). title: Kagome Hulls: six corner-sharing networks of solid clusters in two space-filling lattices, one rule, and its icosahedral exception
description: Two space-filling lattices share the same rock-salt arrangement of cubic cells: the Stella–Jewel Lattice (DICTO Jewels on the even cells, stella octangulas on the odd) and the Sunstar Lattice (regular dodecahedra on the even cells, Dogstars on the odd). Grouping even cells into solid clusters shaped like a convex hull (rhombohedron, cuboctahedron hollow or solid, cube, rhombic dodecahedron, octahedron), we find in both lattices a network in which any two clusters share at most one piece and every shared piece lies in exactly two clusters, corner to corner as in the Kagome and pyrochlore nets. The rhombohedral hull gives a perfect Kagome net, with every piece in exactly two clusters. Across the six hulls one rule holds: a hull with n corners sits on a network where each cluster has n neighbours . The 13-dodecahedron cluster is the exception: its hull has 12 corners, but at most 3 clusters can share corners with it and no lattice exists. The rule breaks where icosahedral symmetry meets periodic space. Corner-sharing octahedra and tetrahedra are known (perovskite, pyrochlore); the clusters of DICTO Jewels and dodecahedra, the rule across six hulls and the exception were not found in a web search (2026-10-09) or in our reference library (2026-10-15). First released inside Kaleidohedra v2026.10.11-octet (DICTO DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23284390); this is its own record. Data, renders and the check outputs are included. title: The DICTO Palintriacontahedron
description: The DICTO Palintriacontahedron is the hull of the icosidodecahedron's central pyramids flipped out at full height: 32 corners and 60 triangles, each half a rhombic-dodecahedron rhombus. It is the member of the dodecahedron–icosahedron hull family with edge ratio exactly 3/√5, in closed form the hull of (0, ±1, ±φ) and ((5 + √5)/6)·{(±1, ±1, ±1), (0, ±φ, ±1/φ)} (cyclic): the rhombic triacontahedron turned inside out.
